items.title: Shift-aware score transport for privacy auditing without retraining
items.summary: Privacy auditing empirically assesses privacy leakage by using membership inference attacks to establish lower bounds on privacy loss. We consider an observational auditing setting in which the auditor cannot insert canaries, control data inclusion, or retrain the target model, and must instead rely on fixed sets of known members and non-members. This setting is relevant for large deployed models or when retraining is restricted by computational or access constraints. In this case, non-members available for auditing may differ in distribution from the training data, causing membership-inference scores to be skewed due to the distribution shift. We address this problem by estimating the counterfactual in-distribution non-member score distribution using the available out-of-distribution (OOD) non-members. Our proposed method learns the relationship between data representations and membership-inference scores from OOD non-members and transports it to the target covariate distribution. Because this transport may become unreliable under extrapolation or imperfect conditional invariance, we further introduce a conservative correction calibrated directly to the nominal transported privacy level. We construct controlled calibration tasks from the available non-member data to estimate how representation-space displacement inflates the audit, and use this estimate to correct the transport-induced audit error. Across multiple datasets with distribution shifts, our method yields substantially more stable privacy estimates while retaining tighter lower bounds than baselines.

items.title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning via Algorithmic Stability
items.summary: Understanding catastrophic forgetting, in which learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned tasks, remains a fundamental challenge in continual learning (CL). Existing theoretical analyses often rely on specific model or task structures and offer limited insight into how iterative optimization affects forgetting. To address this gap, we develop an algorithmic stability framework for expected population forgetting under SGD without prescribing a particular model architecture. Specifically, we decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting. To bound the generalization gaps, we track how a sample perturbation affects updates within a task and propagates through subsequent tasks. We consider constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules. Comparing the two decaying schedules allows us to characterize how restarting learning-rate decay at task boundaries affects the propagation of historical sample perturbations. For empirical forgetting, we derive bounds for all three schedules by retaining cumulative gradient alignment along the optimization trajectory, without requiring convexity. Combining these results yields upper bounds on expected forgetting that capture the effects of training set size, the number of updates per task, the total number of tasks, learning-rate schedules, and cumulative gradient alignment. Finally, we conduct experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet to examine the empirical implications of our theoretical findings.

items.title: Diffusion Language Models for Perplexity-Aware Black-Box Attacks
items.summary: \emph{Continuous-space} attacks find prompts that trigger malicious behaviors, such as overthinking, in black-box LLMs by sampling or optimizing over a low-dimensional Gaussian latent space and decoding it to text through a \emph{random mapping} and nearest-token lookup. Because the random mapping is not learned from language, its prompts can be highly unnatural, and as such easily detectable through input guardrails, and the risk estimates they yield are not grounded in natural prompts. In this paper, we demonstrate that the same continuous latent-space framework can be coupled directly to a learned generative distribution over language, a continuous diffusion language model (dLLM), which removes the artificial random mapping while preserving the standard-Gaussian latent formulation and the downstream sampling or optimization procedure. We evaluate this approach under two settings: sampling-based estimation using \emph{RareTrap} and optimization-based search using \emph{ThinkTrap}. We find that character-level perplexity drops from $10^3$--$10^7$ to 3--5 in RareTrap and from 20--28 to 4.3--5.4 in ThinkTrap. We also find that model risk estimates can differ by an order of magnitude across the two mappings.

items.title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: Online Policy Distillation (OPD) often outperforms offline methods such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) by training on trajectories sampled directly from the student. However, standard OPD trains the student to follow the teacher at every state of the trajectory, assuming that teacher guidance is always beneficial. We instead distinguish between what the teacher prefers and what actually helps the current student succeed. We introduce Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation (AOPD), which weights teacher actions by their counterfactual advantage under the student. Teacher actions that improve the student's expected outcome are reinforced, while those that do not are downweighted. Directly computing these advantages requires trying alternative teacher actions at each step and running new rollouts from each. Instead, we show that the AOPD objective can be estimated using only standard student rollouts and their terminal rewards. Our estimator uses teacher importance weights on the student-sampled actions to provide unbiased advantage-weighted supervision, without any additional rollouts or reward evaluations. This allows AOPD to focus teacher supervision on actions that help the current student while preserving the rollout efficiency of standard OPD. Experiments on math, coding, and Medqa show gains over distillation and RL baselines in both external-teacher and self-distillation settings.

items.title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
items.summary: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.

items.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
items.summary: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.

items.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
items.summary: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.

items.title: CRANE: Post-Hoc Counterfactual Retrieval for Multimodal Classifiers
items.summary: Counterfactual explanation methods have been introduced for unimodal settings, with dedicated frameworks for tabular, timeseries, text, and image data, yet no post-hoc method has been designed for classifiers that learn from multimodal inputs. Existing explainability methods for multimodal classifiers apply modality-specific attribution independently to each input, which fails to yield coherent explanations and does not transfer to arbitrary pre-trained multimodal architectures. To address these shortcomings, we present CRANE (Counterfactual Retrieval via Agnostic Nearest-neighbour Explanations), the first post-hoc, model-agnostic framework for nearest-neighbour multimodal counterfactual generation that retrieves real training examples from the target class as candidate explanations, ensuring plausibility by construction. Across four heterogeneous datasets and three fusion strategies, we show that Multimodal Consensus Retrieval (MC-R), which intersects per-modality neighbour sets to identify instances jointly close to the query in every modality, emerges as the strongest multimodal strategy, achieving the best or joint-best outcome on three of four datasets while grounding every explanation in the joint training distribution. Unimodal strategies remain competitive when a single modality dominates the decision boundary.

items.title: Efficient and Optimal Learning of Discrete Distributions with Person-Level Privacy
items.summary: We study learning a discrete distribution under person-level differential privacy in the batched setting. Given $n$ users, each contributing $m$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $\mu$ over $[k]$, we seek an estimate of $\mu$ with total-variation error $\alpha$. We give polynomial-time algorithms under both pure and approximate differential privacy. Under pure $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(\alpha^2 m)+k/(\alpha\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k/\varepsilon)$, the first polynomial-time pure-DP guarantee matching the information-theoretic optimum up to logarithmic factors. Under approximate $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(\alpha^2 m)+k/(\alpha\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k+\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon)$. At $\delta=2^{-\Theta(k)}$, this is $\widetilde O(k)$ for fixed $\alpha,\varepsilon,m$ and failure probability. Our algorithms use a new degree-6 sum-of-squares estimator for learning from untrusted batches. Its key ingredient is a trace-bounded diagonal majorizer for the difference between the empirical covariance of the repaired batch averages and the multinomial covariance predicted by their mean. We prove that clean data admit this certificate through semidefinite-programming duality and a new application of the stronger symmetric form of Grothendieck's inequality due to Friedland and Lim. The certificate preserves the mean-dependent variance of multinomial batch averages, yielding the near-optimal robust rate $O(\eta\sqrt{\log(1/\eta)/m})$ and providing the score required by the privacy reduction. We also prove a statistical query lower bound ruling out a uniformly smaller order of error under fixed polynomial SQ resource bounds.

items.title: OP-Print: Tracing Membership Imprints in On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.summary: On-policy distillation has been widely adopted for alleviating the distribution mismatch of off-policy distillation. Self-distillation further removes the need for an external teacher by using the student's own outputs, enhanced with extra context or demonstrations, as supervision. This teacher-free design makes on-policy self-distillation practical, yet its privacy risks remain largely unexplored. In particular, using two coupled views of the same training example may strengthen its memorization. Motivated by this, we present the first study of membership inference attacks against on-policy self-distillation. We investigate both gray-box and black-box threat models and propose a unified attack framework, named OP-Print. OP-Print builds on our finding that the supervision imprint in on-policy self-distillation is sparse and structured, concentrating on uncertainty-sensitive correction sites rather than across the entire rollout. Exploiting this property, we construct attack signals tailored to the two access levels: in the gray-box setting, OP-Print directly aggregates the privileged teacher-student residual correction along the same rollout; in the black-box setting, it measures restart-based output-basin stability as an observable surrogate for the hidden correction process. Across diverse models and distillation schemes, all baseline attacks remain essentially at random guessing even under gray-box access, whereas OP-Print is broadly validated to be effective in both gray-box and black-box settings.

items.title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3
items.summary: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

items.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
items.summary: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

items.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
items.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.

items.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
items.summary: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $\epsilon$ hyperparameter.

items.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.

It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.

items.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
items.summary: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

items.title: Why Constrained Updates Still Forget: A Functional-Path Analysis of Continual SFT
items.summary: Supervised fine-tuning adapts language models to specialized tasks but can disrupt previously acquired behavior. Existing approaches constrain parameters, gradients, or replay objectives, yet the connection between the protected object, the intervening trajectory, and retained outputs remains unclear. We develop a functional-path account that decomposes old-loss changes along realized updates into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects. The account yields a conditional refresh budget and identifies the restoring direction supplied by informative replay. Matched QLoRA interventions separate constraint granularity from placement before or after Adam: placement strongly affects retention across the studied code-label audits, whereas the granularity interaction depends on the endpoint. Checkpointed generation separates endpoint recovery from higher sampled-path accuracy, and matched replay schedules reveal loss exposure concealed by final scores. A sequential-task comparison extends this distinction to backward transfer: subspace regularization and projection improve average retention while trading off different old tasks; supervised replay protects both more consistently in this setting. Additional response interfaces distinguish content gains from exact-response retention. These findings connect update-level protection to task-wise behavior and motivate mitigation through explicit functional anchors, trajectory evaluation, and joint old/new auditing.

items.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via Generalized Moment Matching
items.summary: We study $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private synthetic data for arbitrary databases of $n$ records in $[-1,1]^d$ under a specified integral probability metric (IPM). We introduce generalized moment matching, which estimates moments privately, fits a probability measure, and samples synthetic records. A general error theorem applies when moment error controls the target IPM. This framework extends Chebyshev moment matching for $1$-Wasserstein distance and smooth queries. We apply the framework to maximum mean discrepancy with Matern and Laplace kernels and a two-layer ReLU neural tangent kernel.We also obtain guarantees for sliced Wasserstein-$1$ and the IPM induced by norm-bounded ReLU networks. With sufficiently many synthetic records,these rates are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed dimension.

items.title: High-Value Training Data from Noisy, Diverse Sources
items.summary: Training state-of-the-art models increasingly requires learning from large, heterogeneous datasets whose examples vary in quality, domain relevance, and source of supervision. Dataweighting---assigning different weights to training examples---offers a general way to control how such data influences training, but learning effective weights at scale remains challenging. We develop a scalable approach to learning dataweights: given a small, high-quality target dataset, we use metagradients through the training process to efficiently optimize training-example weights directly for performance on the target domain. To scale beyond a fixed dataset and model, we learn parametric weighting rules that generalize to new and streaming examples and transfer from smaller models to substantially larger ones. We study reward modeling as a prototypical application, where preference data may be noisy, adversarial, synthetic, or mismatched with the target domain. Learned dataweights improve held-out performance, automatically adapt reward models to specialized domains, and allow mixtures of human and synthetic supervision to outperform either source alone.

items.title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
items.summary: Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.

items.title: xVGAE: A Hierarchical Variational Graph Autoencoder for Exchangeable Graphs
items.summary: Graphs play a crucial role in many applications, ranging from drug discovery to social network modeling and astronomy. Generative models for graphs have substantially advanced in recent years, but we identify relatively simple scenarios where state-of-the-art models struggle to converge within a standard compute budget, or exhibit prohibitively slow generation times. We propose a generative architecture that achieves quality competitive with state-of-the-art models and is orders of magnitude faster at generation. Our approach is inspired by the Aldous-Hoover theorem, a classic representation theorem that characterizes any probability distribution of graphs that is invariant to permutations of node indices or exchangeable. This theorem establishes that three ingredients suffice: a graph-level latent variable, a set of exchangeable node-specific latent variables, and a so-called graphon function that maps graph- and node-level variables to the probability of an edge between any node pair. Given a training set of graphs, our exchangeable Variational Graph AutoEncoder (xVGAE) learns an approximation to their underlying graphons, as well as graph- and node-level latent variables. We show that our xVGAE encodes latent representations that correlate with graph- and node-level properties, and can (quickly, in one shot) generate new graphs that closely match key training set statistics.

items.title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
items.summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.

items.title: Random Projections for Spectral Algorithms: Optimal Rates in Sobolev Norms
items.summary: Random projections (RP) offer an effective method for reducing computational and storage overhead while preserving the geometric structure of data. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the optimal generalization performance of specific kernel-regularized algorithms with RP in the well-specified setting and under restrictive conditions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of the generalization performance of RP-based spectral algorithms under general conditions \change{without sacrificing statistical efficiency}. By leveraging the embedding property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and a refined analysis of the operator similarity, we establish optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms that match the minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. For two common implementations of RP, randomized sketches and Nystr\"{o}m sub-sampling (uniform or leverage-based), we show that the projection dimension required for optimality is proportional to the average or maximal effective dimension, yielding a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining the statistical efficiency. Our results do not rely on the uniform boundedness assumption on the regression function and are valid across a wide range of source conditions, i.e., $s> \alpha_0-1/\beta$, where $s,\beta$, and $\alpha_0$ denote the smoothness index, capacity index, and the embedding index, respectively. In the benign case when $\alpha_0=1/\beta$, the optimality holds for all $s\in (0,2\tau]$ with $\tau$ and $\gamma$ denoting the qualification index and norm index. Experimental results demonstrate both the theoretical validity and the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.

items.title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
items.summary: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

items.title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
items.summary: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

items.title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
items.summary: We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.

items.title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
items.summary: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.

items.title: Nonparametric autoregressive estimation of probability distributions with parallel gradient boosting
items.summary: Nonparametric estimation of joint probability distributions is a core problem in statistics, which is notoriously challenging with high-dimensional data. Such challenges also arise with conditional distribution estimation and have led to flexible algorithms that aim to tackle the ''curse of dimensionality'' by exploiting predictive structures of lower dimension than the ambient space. In this paper, we study the use of such conditional distribution estimators to estimate joint distributions by factorizing the latter in an ''autoregressive'' way. We show that for loss functions satisfying a subadditivity property, bounds on the convergence rate of an autoregressive estimator can be derived from bounds on the convergence rate of the conditional distribution estimators. These bounds relate the difficulty of estimating the joint distribution to that of estimating the most challenging factor in the autoregressive factorization. When the conditional estimators adapt to sparsity in their conditioning sets, we characterize this difficulty through variable elimination in an undirected dependence graph. This allows bounding the rates of convergence by quantities related to the sparsity of the graph, and provides an additional motivation for the autoregressive approach. We then evaluate the practical performance of an autoregressive estimator based on parallel gradient boosting, a flexible nonparametric method for estimating conditional distributions. The estimator demonstrates competitive estimation performance on various simulated and real datasets, even without optimizing the factorization order. Together, these results support nonparametric autoregressive estimation as a practical approach to flexible joint distribution estimation.

Abstract: Nonparametric estimation of joint probability distributions is a core problem in statistics, which is notoriously challenging with high-dimensional data. Such challenges also arise with conditional distribution estimation and have led to flexible algorithms that aim to tackle the ''curse of dimensionality'' by exploiting predictive structures of lower dimension than the ambient space. In this paper, we study the use of such conditional distribution estimators to estimate joint distributions by factorizing the latter in an ''autoregressive'' way. We show that for loss functions satisfying a subadditivity property, bounds on the convergence rate of an autoregressive estimator can be derived from bounds on the convergence rate of the conditional distribution estimators. These bounds relate the difficulty of estimating the joint distribution to that of estimating the most challenging factor in the autoregressive factorization. When the conditional estimators adapt to sparsity in their conditioning sets, we characterize this difficulty through variable elimination in an undirected dependence graph. This allows bounding the rates of convergence by quantities related to the sparsity of the graph, and provides an additional motivation for the autoregressive approach. We then evaluate the practical performance of an autoregressive estimator based on parallel gradient boosting, a flexible nonparametric method for estimating conditional distributions. The estimator demonstrates competitive estimation performance on various simulated and real datasets, even without optimizing the factorization order. Together, these results support nonparametric autoregressive estimation as a practical approach to flexible joint distribution estimation.

items.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
items.summary: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

items.title: Q&A: How AI came to model the “messy” human mind
items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. To mimic creative thinking, these AI pioneers intentionally injected randomness into algorithms designed to deterministically solve problems, Lindquist writes in a new paper that appears in the journal Past and Present. In the paper, he traces the origins of AI hallucinations back to this early research and suggests there will be inevitable tradeoffs between creativity and predictability when trying to build machines that mimic human behavior. MIT News spoke with Lindquist about these ideas. Q: Why did early computer engineers believe they needed to inject randomness and irrationality into AI systems designed for logic and calculation? A: There is a long history of many figures in the world of science and art theorizing that chance plays an important part in discovery and creativity — in the ability to originate ideas. They equated creativity with unexpected leaps of logic, or even a dream-like state that allows you to think about things from a new perspective. In the early 1950s, one popular idea from John Pierce, who was a prominent electrical engineer at Bell Labs, was about math being valuable in the world of art. The idea was shared by a lot of people working in early computing. When we think of artwork that includes math, we may think of something very orderly and precise, but Pierce came to the opposite conclusion. He concluded that the utility of math is that it could remove order from art. Then in a very calculated way, math could add a burst of the unexpected as a means to deviate from clichés and add an element of irregularity which just might lead to insight. One popular way to add irregularity into otherwise predictable computers was through artificial (or random) neural networks . Many early neural networks were built by psychologists, who thought that by enabling scientists to build a model of the brain, artificial neural networks allowed scientists to observe what is happening inside, including how brains make productive mistakes. Rather than being black boxes, researchers believed these systems could open this black box of the mind and let scientists peer inside and see all the messy stuff that was really happening. But there was another camp in the world of AI who thought that creative thinking was just “normal” thinking done better. It is interesting to look at these two very simplistic heuristics for understanding intelligence and creativity, and how they do and don’t mesh. The debate, then, was about trying to determine what human inventiveness boils down to, and then how to reconstitute human inventiveness in machine form. Q: How did these early computer engineers view AI, and how is it different from the way we think about AI today? A: When we think of AI systems, we think of ChatGPT or Claude. We value and use these systems because they give answers that, most of the time, are correct. One of the things that was most interesting to me in this research was finding out that a lot of the early advocates of these systems valued them for exactly the opposite reason. They wanted a system that, on occasion, gave answers that deviated from their expectations. They already had systems that could deliver reasonable and expected answers. They saw neural networks as valuable because they could give unexpected, perhaps even strange and bizarre answers. One reason we might view these systems differently today could be because of how they operate. Early on, these systems were confined to laboratories, so there weren’t really any real-world consequences of a system that gives a strange, or wrong, output. But now there are legal and monetary reasons why OpenAI or Anthropic doesn’t want a chatbot that gives unexpected or creative answers. There has been a “sanding down” of strangeness in these systems. They still potentially have that at their core, but it is something that is now largely suppressed. Q: How did early neural networks that incorporated randomness to simulate human creativity evolve to become the dominant paradigm in AI? A: For a long time, a specific kind of AI called “symbolic AI” was the dominant approach. Essentially, symbolic AI says the world is based on rules. The role of the AI researcher is to try and reconstruct the knowledge of the world in facts and propositions and feed it into a computer. Neural networks, with their use of randomness to solve problems, started to gain traction in the 1950s but fell out favor early on. Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist who was a very important early figure in neural networks, died prematurely; he died accidentally on his 43rd birthday in 1971. He was quite a charismatic and forceful personality, who made a lot of grand promises about what systems based on neural networks could do. By the time he died, a shift toward symbolic AI was already underway. It is possible if, had he lived, things might have turned out differently. But neural networks never went away. By the 1980s they had shifted more into the world of cognitive science. To become more powerful, and more useful, neural networks needed a lot of data and computational power. That didn’t really arrive until the advent of the internet, when a lot of data became available and computing started to power up. Around 2012, neural networks started to outperform and outpace a statistical form of machine learning, and they kept growing from there. Q: What lessons can we learn from studying AI’s history that could inform its development? A: I think there is a cautionary lesson here. The ideas and experiences of these early engineers tell us that we can work toward quashing hallucinations — we can work toward making AI perform a certain way so it doesn’t produce unexpected or unwanted answers — but there are going to be other consequences of that. These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.

items.title: The Decentralized GPU Marketplace: Breaking the Big Tech Compute Monopoly
items.summary: High-end AI chips sit mostly in data centers owned or leased by a handful of hyperscalers, and in 2026 that capacity got more expensive, not less. Decentralized compute networks such as Akash, io.net, and Render pool GPUs from independent operators and sell them in an open market. Listed H100 prices run roughly 50 to 80 percent below hyperscaler on-demand rates, depending on which day and which source you check. The savings are real for inference, fine-tuning, batch jobs, and anything that fits on one machine. Large-scale training across the open internet is still an unsolved engineering problem. Latency, node churn, mixed hardware, and trust all get in the way. My read: these networks will not replace the hyperscalers. They set a price floor and give independent builders a second option, which is already a meaningful shift. Read All

items.title: Anthropic’s Elevator Problem: Persuading Investors to Share Its AI Dream
items.summary: One quotation has rattled around in my head for a while, which I first heard from early Anthropic investor Jaan Tallinn: “The future of the world will be decided by a group of people who fit in an elevator.” The enigmatic billionaire said on a podcast earlier this year that a friend had used the illustration to describe the concentration of power at the leading AI companies. I’ve been reflecting on it as Anthropic prepares for its Wall Street debut because the company’s small group of powerful insiders, who are set to realize incredible wealth at unprecedented speed, face their biggest test in explaining themselves to the world outside their elevator. To raise the money Anthropic leaders need, and to keep raising it again and again, big fund managers need to fully buy in.

items.title: From Keywords to Meaning: How Embeddings Power Semantic Search in AI
items.summary: Part 6 of the Production RAG Series — Why Keyword Stuffing Fails in the AI Era, How Embeddings Turn Language into Math, and What Dimensions Really Mean. Hey friends! Welcome back to our ongoing series on building production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In Part 5: Advanced RAG Chunking , we explored how to break complex documents into clean, retrievable units using architectures like Parent-Document Retrieval, Breadcrumbs, and Contextual Retrieval. Now that our documents are neatly chunked and enriched with metadata, we face the next big puzzle: How do we actually search through them? Have you ever noticed how sellers on online marketplaces or creators on YouTube write their titles? Take a look at a typical product title on an e-commerce site: Wireless Noise-Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones with Microphone — Bluetooth Travel Headset, 40-Hour Battery Or a popular programming tutorial on YouTube: Python Full Course for Beginners [2026] | Learn Python in 8 Hours Notice what the creators are doing: The headphone seller doesn’t just write “Headphones” ; they also add “Headset” , “Over-Ear” , and “Wireless” . The tutorial creator includes “Full Course” , “Beginners” , “Learn Python” , and adds video tags like “Python tutorial” and “coding crash course” . Why do they do this? Are they just being repetitive? Not at all. They do it because of how traditional search engines work . For decades, search systems have heavily relied on Keyword Search (lexical matching). Traditional search engines like Elasticsearch or Solr use techniques like stemming (matching “run”, “running”, and “runner”), category filters, and curated synonym lists. However, keyword matching is still an important part of how these systems find and rank results. If a customer searches for “headset” and a product is only described as “headphones”, the search engine may need a synonym rule or another signal to connect the two. Creators and sellers include related terms in their titles and tags to increase the chances of matching what users search for. We spent decades adapting to this: typing keyword-heavy phrases into search bars like “ best coffee shop downtown wifi open late” . And then, AI changed how we interact with software. 🗣️ The Shift: Humans Don’t Speak in Keywords Anymore Today, people don’t interact with systems using robotic keywords. They talk to AI assistants the same way they talk to another human being — using full, natural sentences. And that exposes a massive problem. Imagine three different customers trying to get help from an e-commerce support system: Customer A says: “Get me a refund.” Customer B says: “I want my money back.” Customer C says: “Please reverse the charge on my card.” Notice something fascinating: “ Same core intent, but entirely different vocabulary!” All three customers want the exact same outcome . Their underlying intent is identical. Yet, they express it through completely different words: Customer A uses the term “ refund ” . Customer B says “ money back ” . Customer C asks to “ reverse the charge ” . Here lies the classic vocabulary mismatch problem of keyword search: If your company’s knowledge base or help center explains the return policy using the word “refund”, a customer searching for “money back” might not find that document easily. Unless the search system accounts for these variations through synonyms or other techniques, the customer could see irrelevant results, find the right policy buried further down the list, or get no useful results at all. And as an engineering team, you cannot realistically anticipate every way a human might express the same thought. Slang, colloquial phrasings, idioms, typos, and different mental models make it impossible to cover every variation through manual keyword stuffing and hand-crafted synonym dictionaries. This is why we desperately need Semantic Search — search based on meaning and intent , not whether the user and the author happened to pick the exact same words. 🤖 The Catch: Computers Don’t Understand Language Like We Do Here is the grand irony of computer science: Humans understand meaning effortlessly. A ten-year-old child instinctively knows that “I want my money back” and “Give me a refund” mean the same thing. Computers have zero intuition. At its core, a computer doesn’t speak English, Spanish, or Hindi. It doesn’t even know what a “dog” or an “apple” is. A computer is simply a magnificent calculating machine. It is extraordinarily good at one thing: doing arithmetic with numbers. So if we want a computer to compare the meaning of two sentences, we face a fundamental roadblock: How do you translate abstract human thoughts into numbers that a computer can calculate? This is where embedding models come in. 🧠 Enter the Embedding Model: Turning Meaning into Math An Embedding Model is a specialized neural network trained on billions of sentences from books, articles, code, and conversations across the web. Instead of memorizing rigid grammar rules, the model learns the subtle relationships between words based on the contexts in which they appear. When you pass a sentence into an embedding model, it analyzes the entire context and transforms that human text into a Vector Representation — which is simply a mathematical term for a list of numbers . Human Sentence: “I want my money back” │ ▼ [ Embedding Model ] │ ▼ Vector Representation (Coordinates in “Meaning Space”): [ 0.34, -0.71, 0.82, 0.15, -0.09, 0.63, … ] The Intuitive Mental Model: The GPS of Human Ideas How do you describe where your favorite restaurant is without writing a poem about its location? You give someone its GPS coordinates : [Latitude: 37.7749° N, Longitude: 122.4194° W] If another coffee shop is right across the street, its GPS coordinates will be almost identical: [37.7750, -122.4195]. If a restaurant is located on the other side of the planet in Tokyo, its coordinates will be vastly different. An embedding vector is a bit like a GPS coordinate in “ Meaning Space. ” When two sentences have similar meanings, their vectors often end up close together — even if they share very few words. Note: GPS coordinates represent physical locations, while embedding coordinates represent patterns learned from language. The individual dimensions don’t have simple meanings like latitude and longitude. 🔍 What a Vector Actually Looks Like (And Why It Works) Let’s look at what actually happens under the hood when we embed our earlier customer refund examples: Sentence 1: "I want my money back" Vector: [ 0.342, -0.715, 0.821, 0.154, ... 0.092 ] Sentence 2: "Get me a refund" Vector: [ 0.351, -0.702, 0.808, 0.149, ... 0.088 ] Sentence 3: "How do I bake sourdough bread?" Vector: [-0.884, 0.129, -0.453, -0.612, ... -0.741 ] These numbers are illustrative examples, not actual outputs from an embedding model. Look closely at the first two vectors. The vector for “I want my money back” and the vector for “Get me a refund” are almost identical, representing the idea that the sentences have similar meanings. The sourdough sentence, on the other hand, represents a completely different topic and would typically be farther away in the embedding space. The computer doesn’t need to rely only on exact word matches. It compares the numerical representations to find text that is semantically similar. That’s the basic idea behind semantic search! 🍎 Demystifying “Dimensions”: The Fruit Stand Analogy Whenever people discuss embeddings, they quickly drop technical jargon like: We are projecting tokens into a 1536-dimensional vector space. It sounds like science fiction. You try to imagine what a 1536-dimensional room looks like, and your head starts spinning. Let’s demystify dimensions using something everyone understands: a fruit stand . Imagine you want to describe different fruits to a computer using only three measurable attributes (three dials): Sweetness (0 to 10) Sourness (0 to 10) Crunchiness (0 to 10) These three attributes are your dimensions. Every fruit gets a 3-number coordinate [Sweetness, Sourness, Crunchiness]: An Apple [8, 2, 9] and a Pear [8, 1, 8] have almost the same numbers. They are sweet, low in sourness, and crunchy. A Lemon [1, 9, 2] has very low sweetness, high sourness, and low crunchiness. It lands far away from the apple. Now, what if you want to distinguish between a red apple and a green Granny Smith apple? 3 dimensions aren’t enough. You add more dials: Dimension 4: Tartness Dimension 5: Color Hue Dimension 6: Juiciness In this example, each dimension represents a specific attribute because we designed it that way just to give you a feel of dimensions. Real embedding models are different. Their dimensions are learned from data, and an individual dimension doesn’t necessarily correspond to a clear attribute like sentiment, formality, tense, domain, topic, or intent. The numbers work together to represent patterns in language. The fruit analogy helps us understand why having more dimensions can provide more room to represent information, without implying that real embedding dimensions are human-readable dials. ⚖️ The Dimension Trade-off: 768 vs. 1536 Dimensions When building real-world AI applications, you will often have to choose between models with different vector sizes. Two common embedding sizes are: 768 dimensions (Common in open-source models like bge-base, all-mpnet-base-v2, e5-base-v2) 1536 dimensions (Common in models like OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small or text-embedding-ada-002) (And up to 3072 dimensions in models like text-embedding-3-large) A common beginner assumption is: “1536 is double 768, so it must be twice as good! Always use 1536!” In engineering, nothing comes without a trade-off. Let’s look at what that choice actually means: Let’s break down what each of these rows actually means in practice: 1. Representation Depth: What Do More Numbers Buy You? Think of dimensions as the number of values available to represent something. In our fruit analogy, three dials give us three values to describe each fruit. Adding more dials lets us represent additional attributes. Similarly, a 768-dimensional embedding contains 768 numbers, while a 1536-dimensional embedding contains twice as many. But here’s the important part: more dimensions don’t automatically mean better semantic understanding. The embedding model learns how to represent language during training. A well-trained 768-dimensional model may outperform a 1536-dimensional model on a particular task. If you’re working with legal documents, medical papers, customer support queries, or e-commerce catalogs, the right way to choose is to test how well different models retrieve the information your application actually needs. Don’t assume that a larger vector will automatically capture more useful nuance for your specific data. 2. The Storage Math: Where Does the ~3.0 KB vs ~6.1 KB Come From? In software, each number in an embedding vector is often stored as a 32-bit floating-point number (Float32). In computer memory, 1 Float32 = 4 bytes. For a 768-dimensional vector: 768 numbers × 4 bytes = 3,072 bytes ≈ 3.1 KB For a 1536-dimensional vector: 1536 numbers × 4 bytes = 6,144 bytes ≈ 6.1 KB Doubling the dimensions doubles the memory required to store each vector when using the same numeric format. 3. RAM Footprint: The Hidden Database Cost Depending on the database and index configuration, vectors may need to be held in memory for fast search. If you have 1,000,000 chunks : At 768 dimensions, the raw vectors occupy ~3.07 GB of RAM. At 1536 dimensions, they occupy ~6.14 GB of RAM. Now imagine your company grows and indexes 20 million chunks (support tickets, Slack messages, emails, wikis). At 1536 dimensions, the raw vectors alone would occupy about 122.88 GB if stored as Float32. That’s a substantial amount of data to store and search. The actual infrastructure also needs space for indexes and other data. 4. Computation Latency: Speed of Comparison When calculating how close two vectors are, the computer must multiply each dimension pairwise (a1×b1+a2×b2+ … + aₙ × bₙ) and sum them up. A 1536-dimensional comparison requires twice as many multiplications and additions as a 768-dimensional comparison. When searching large collections of vectors, that extra arithmetic can increase computation cost and contribute to higher retrieval latency. The Rule of Thumb: Don’t default to the largest model just because the number looks impressive. Start by evaluating a suitable embedding model on your data. Compare retrieval quality, storage needs, and performance, then choose the dimensions that provide the best trade-off for your application. 🎯 The Inference: How Matching Actually Happens in Real Time Now that we understand how embeddings represent text, let’s step into the shoes of our application when a user actually asks a question. Here is the step-by-step journey: How Do We Actually Calculate “Similarity”? How do we measure which stored vector is mathematically closest to the user’s query vector? There are a few ways to measure distance between points in math: Euclidean Distance (L2 Distance): Measuring straight-line distance between two points. Dot Product: Multiplying corresponding numbers and adding the results. Cosine Similarity: Measuring the angle between two vectors. Cosine similarity is a common choice for text search, although the best metric depends on the embedding model and how its vectors are used. Why is cosine similarity so useful? Let’s use the Flashlight Analogy. Imagine two people standing in a pitch-black circular arena holding flashlights: Direction of the beam: Think of this as the direction of the vector. When two vectors point in similar directions, their cosine similarity is high. Length of the beam: A vector also has a magnitude, or length. But vector magnitude doesn’t simply tell us how long the original text is. If you used straight-line distance (Euclidean distance), two vectors could be far apart because of their magnitudes, even when they point in the same direction. Cosine similarity focuses on the angle between the two vectors rather than their magnitudes. If both vectors point in the exact same direction (θ = 0°), the score is 1.0 (A perfect semantic match). If they point at right angles (θ = 90°), the score is 0.0 (Completely unrelated topics). If they point in opposite directions (θ = 180°), the score is -1.0 (Direct opposites). Cosine Similarity = (A · B) / (‖A‖ × ‖B‖) By measuring the cosine angle, your system easily matches a casual 4-word user question with a detailed 300-word documentation chunk without getting misled by length. 💥 The Next Big Wall: How Do We Actually Store & Search Millions of Vectors? Let’s take a breath and look at what we’ve built. We solved the keyword search problem: our system understands meaning , not just characters. We transformed our messy company documents into neat mathematical vectors. When a user asks a question, we convert their question into a vector and use Cosine Similarity to find the best match. Everything looks complete on paper. Until you launch it into production. Imagine your company has 1,000,000 document chunks. You might think: “Why can’t I just store these vectors in my existing MySQL or PostgreSQL database? I’ll just create a table with an array column!” -- The intuitive thought: CREATE TABLE document_chunks ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, content TEXT, embedding FLOAT[1536] ); When a user asks a question, how does the database find the 5 closest vectors? To understand why this is a nightmare for a traditional database, we have to look at how database indexes actually work. How a Normal Database Index Works (The Dictionary Analogy) Imagine you want to find the definition of the word “Robot” in a physical English dictionary. You don’t start on page 1 and read every single word until you reach “R”. You flip straight to the letter “R” in the middle of the book. Why can you do that? Because the entire dictionary is organised along a single line of order : from A to Z . Traditional database indexes (most famously, the B-Tree) work on a similar principle. When you index a column like user_id, price, or created_at, the database organizes the values so it can quickly find the entries it needs. For example: Smallest numbers to largest numbers (1 < 2 < 3 … < 100) Dates from oldest to newest (Jan 1 → Dec 31) Names from A to Z (Alice → Bob → Charlie) Because the data is neatly sorted in one direction, if you run WHERE price < 50, the database instantly jumps to 50 and ignores the entire rest of the table. It skips 99% of the work. Why Vectors Make This More Challenging Now look at an embedding vector. It doesn’t have just one number or one word. It has 1536 numbers all at the same time : Vector A: [ 0.82, -0.15, 0.44, 0.19, ... ] Vector B: [ 0.81, -0.12, 0.50, 0.08, ... ] Vector C: [ 0.79, -0.30, 0.41, 0.22, ... ] Now ask yourself a deceptively simple question: How would you put these vectors in a single sorted order that makes it easy to find the nearest ones? Is Vector A “greater than” Vector B? Well, on Dimension 1, A is bigger(0.82 > 0.81). But on Dimension 2, B is bigger(-0.12 > -0.15). And on Dimension 3, B is bigger again (0.50 > 0.44). There is no natural “A to Z” order in a 1536-dimensional space! You cannot line up multi-dimensional coordinates along a single straight line from smallest to largest. Traditional B-Tree indexes aren’t designed to find the nearest neighbors of a high-dimensional vector. For that, we need a different kind of search index. The Full Table Scan Challenge Without a suitable vector index, the database may need to compare the query vector against every stored vector. For each row, it calculates a similarity or distance score, then ranks the results to find the closest matches. Load Row 1 → compute cosine similarity across 1536 numbers. Load Row 2 → compute cosine similarity across 1536 numbers. Repeat for all 1,000,000 rows . Sort the 1,000,000 calculated scores to find the top 5. Let’s do the math on what happens during a single search: 1,000,000 chunks × 1536 dimensions = 1.536 billion vector-component comparisons. If many users search at the same time, that work can add up and increase CPU usage and response times. Traditional B-Tree indexes aren’t designed for this kind of nearest-neighbor search. However, that doesn’t mean you can’t use a relational database for vector search. For example, PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension supports both exact vector search and specialized approximate-nearest-neighbor indexes. To search large collections of high-dimensional vectors efficiently, we need an approach designed for finding nearest neighbors. 👉 The Vector Database — n Part 7 , we will dive into this exact mystery: How Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search makes vector retrieval faster by searching a promising subset of vectors rather than comparing every vector. The magic of HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs: how algorithms build high-speed expressways through high-dimensional space. The Big Architectural Decision : When should you use a dedicated vector database (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate), and when is PostgreSQL with pgvector all you will ever need? See you in Part 7! 💬 Let’s Chat! Did the difference between keywords and semantic embeddings resonate with problems you’ve faced? Are you currently using 768 or 1536 dimensions in your pipeline? Let’s talk about your search challenges in the comments below! From Keywords to Meaning: How Embeddings Power Semantic Search in AI was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

⚖️ The Dimension Trade-off: 768 vs. 1536 Dimensions

  • 768 dimensions (Common in open-source models like bge-base, all-mpnet-base-v2, e5-base-v2)
  • 1536 dimensions (Common in models like OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small or text-embedding-ada-002)
  • (And up to 3072 dimensions in models like text-embedding-3-large)

A common beginner assumption is: “1536 is double 768, so it must be twice as good! Always use 1536!”

In engineering, nothing comes without a trade-off. Let’s look at what that choice actually means:

Let’s break down what each of these rows actually means in practice:

1. Representation Depth: What Do More Numbers Buy You?

Think of dimensions as the number of values available to represent something.

In our fruit analogy, three dials give us three values to describe each fruit. Adding more dials lets us represent additional attributes. Similarly, a 768-dimensional embedding contains 768 numbers, while a 1536-dimensional embedding contains twice as many.

But here’s the important part: more dimensions don’t automatically mean better semantic understanding.

The embedding model learns how to represent language during training. A well-trained 768-dimensional model may outperform a 1536-dimensional model on a particular task.

Don’t assume that a larger vector will automatically capture more useful nuance for your specific data.
