In software, each number in an embedding vector is often stored as a 32-bit floating-point number (Float32). In computer memory, 1 Float32 = 4 bytes.

For a 768-dimensional vector: 768 numbers × 4 bytes = 3,072 bytes ≈ 3.1 KB

For a 1536-dimensional vector: 1536 numbers × 4 bytes = 6,144 bytes ≈ 6.1 KB

Doubling the dimensions doubles the memory required to store each vector when using the same numeric format.

3. RAM Footprint: The Hidden Database Cost

Depending on the database and index configuration, vectors may need to be held in memory for fast search.

If you have 1,000,000 chunks:

  • At 768 dimensions, the raw vectors occupy ~3.07 GB of RAM.
  • At 1536 dimensions, they occupy ~6.14 GB of RAM.

Now imagine your company grows and indexes 20 million chunks (support tickets, Slack messages, emails, wikis). At 1536 dimensions, the raw vectors alone would occupy about 122.88 GB if stored as Float32.

That’s a substantial amount of data to store and search. The actual infrastructure also needs space for indexes and other data.

4. Computation Latency: Speed of Comparison

When calculating how close two vectors are, the computer must multiply each dimension pairwise (a1×b1+a2×b2+ … + aₙ × bₙ) and sum them up.

A 1536-dimensional comparison requires twice as many multiplications and additions as a 768-dimensional comparison.

When searching large collections of vectors, that extra arithmetic can increase computation cost and contribute to higher retrieval latency.

The Rule of Thumb:

Don’t default to the largest model just because the number looks impressive. Start by evaluating a suitable embedding model on your data. Compare retrieval quality, storage needs, and performance, then choose the dimensions that provide the best trade-off for your application.

🎯 The Inference: How Matching Actually Happens in Real Time

Now that we understand how embeddings represent text, let’s step into the shoes of our application when a user actually asks a question.

Here is the step-by-step journey:

How Do We Actually Calculate “Similarity”?

How do we measure which stored vector is mathematically closest to the user’s query vector?

There are a few ways to measure distance between points in math:

  • Euclidean Distance (L2 Distance): Measuring straight-line distance between two points.
  • Dot Product: Multiplying corresponding numbers and adding the results.
  • Cosine Similarity: Measuring the angle between two vectors.

Cosine similarity is a common choice for text search, although the best metric depends on the embedding model and how its vectors are used.

Why is cosine similarity so useful?

Let’s use the Flashlight Analogy.

Imagine two people standing in a pitch-black circular arena holding flashlights:

  • Direction of the beam: Think of this as the direction of the vector. When two vectors point in similar directions, their cosine similarity is high.
  • Length of the beam: A vector also has a magnitude, or length. But vector magnitude doesn’t simply tell us how long the original text is.

If you used straight-line distance (Euclidean distance), two vectors could be far apart because of their magnitudes, even when they point in the same direction.

Cosine similarity focuses on the angle between the two vectors rather than their magnitudes.

  • If both vectors point in the exact same direction (θ = 0°), the score is 1.0 (A perfect semantic match).
  • If they point at right angles (θ = 90°), the score is 0.0 (Completely unrelated topics).
  • If they point in opposite directions (θ = 180°), the score is -1.0 (Direct opposites).

Cosine Similarity = (A · B) / (‖A‖ × ‖B‖)

By measuring the cosine angle, your system easily matches a casual 4-word user question with a detailed 300-word documentation chunk without getting misled by length.

💥 The Next Big Wall: How Do We Actually Store & Search Millions of Vectors?

Let’s take a breath and look at what we’ve built.

  1. We solved the keyword search problem: our system understands meaning, not just characters.
  2. We transformed our messy company documents into neat mathematical vectors.
  3. When a user asks a question, we convert their question into a vector and use Cosine Similarity to find the best match.

Everything looks complete on paper. Until you launch it into production.

Imagine your company has 1,000,000 document chunks.

You might think:
“Why can’t I just store these vectors in my existing MySQL or PostgreSQL database? I’ll just create a table with an array column!”

-- The intuitive thought:
CREATE TABLE document_chunks (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    content TEXT,
    embedding FLOAT[1536]
);

When a user asks a question, how does the database find the 5 closest vectors? To understand why this is a nightmare for a traditional database, we have to look at how database indexes actually work.

How a Normal Database Index Works (The Dictionary Analogy)

Imagine you want to find the definition of the word “Robot” in a physical English dictionary. You don’t start on page 1 and read every single word until you reach “R”. You flip straight to the letter “R” in the middle of the book. Why can you do that? Because the entire dictionary is organised along a single line of order: from A to Z.

Traditional database indexes (most famously, the B-Tree) work on a similar principle. When you index a column like user_id, price, or created_at, the database organizes the values so it can quickly find the entries it needs.

For example:

  • Smallest numbers to largest numbers (1 < 2 < 3 … < 100)
  • Dates from oldest to newest (Jan 1 → Dec 31)
  • Names from A to Z (Alice → Bob → Charlie)

Because the data is neatly sorted in one direction, if you run WHERE price < 50, the database instantly jumps to 50 and ignores the entire rest of the table. It skips 99% of the work.

Why Vectors Make This More Challenging

Now look at an embedding vector. It doesn’t have just one number or one word. It has 1536 numbers all at the same time:

Vector A:  [ 0.82, -0.15,  0.44,  0.19, ... ]
Vector B:  [ 0.81, -0.12,  0.50,  0.08, ... ]
Vector C:  [ 0.79, -0.30,  0.41,  0.22, ... ]

Now ask yourself a deceptively simple question: How would you put these vectors in a single sorted order that makes it easy to find the nearest ones?

  • Is Vector A “greater than” Vector B?
  • Well, on Dimension 1, A is bigger(0.82 > 0.81).
  • But on Dimension 2, B is bigger(-0.12 > -0.15).
  • And on Dimension 3, B is bigger again (0.50 > 0.44).

There is no natural “A to Z” order in a 1536-dimensional space! You cannot line up multi-dimensional coordinates along a single straight line from smallest to largest.

Traditional B-Tree indexes aren’t designed to find the nearest neighbors of a high-dimensional vector. For that, we need a different kind of search index.

The Full Table Scan Challenge

Without a suitable vector index, the database may need to compare the query vector against every stored vector. For each row, it calculates a similarity or distance score, then ranks the results to find the closest matches.

  • Load Row 1 → compute cosine similarity across 1536 numbers.
  • Load Row 2 → compute cosine similarity across 1536 numbers.
  • Repeat for all 1,000,000 rows.
  • Sort the 1,000,000 calculated scores to find the top 5.

Let’s do the math on what happens during a single search:

1,000,000 chunks × 1536 dimensions = 1.536 billion vector-component comparisons.

If many users search at the same time, that work can add up and increase CPU usage and response times.

Traditional B-Tree indexes aren’t designed for this kind of nearest-neighbor search. However, that doesn’t mean you can’t use a relational database for vector search. For example, PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension supports both exact vector search and specialized approximate-nearest-neighbor indexes.

To search large collections of high-dimensional vectors efficiently, we need an approach designed for finding nearest neighbors.

👉 The Vector Database —

n Part 7, we will dive into this exact mystery:

  • How Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search makes vector retrieval faster by searching a promising subset of vectors rather than comparing every vector.
  • The magic of HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs: how algorithms build high-speed expressways through high-dimensional space.
  • The Big Architectural Decision: When should you use a dedicated vector database (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate), and when is PostgreSQL with pgvector all you will ever need?

See you in Part 7!

💬 Let’s Chat!

Did the difference between keywords and semantic embeddings resonate with problems you’ve faced? Are you currently using 768 or 1536 dimensions in your pipeline? Let’s talk about your search challenges in the comments below!

From Keywords to Meaning: How Embeddings Power Semantic Search in AI was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Why Blackstone Thinks AI Bottlenecks Could Work in its Favor
items.summary: Greetings! On their earnings calls earlier in the week, Meta Platforms and SpaceX delivered the same underlying message to investors: demand for AI is running ahead of the supply of AI compute. On Thursday, another important player in the AI ecosystem—Blackstone, the alternative asset management giant—repeated a version of that refrain. On its own earnings call, the firm, a major investor at the center of the AI data center boom, faced pointed questions from analysts about rising financing costs and mounting investor concerns over the sustainability of the buildout. Its executives argued that the very factors threatening the AI industry’s expansion could actually work in Blackstone’s favor. CEO Steve Schwarzman noted that constraints on power availability and growing public opposition to new data centers are making it harder to bring new capacity online, potentially making existing facilities more valuable. Blackstone President Jon Gray also suggested the firm could seek higher returns on projects where it hasn’t signed leases yet in order to offset rising borrowing costs. Blackstone’s third-quarter results offered some support for that argument: Its infrastructure investments were buoyed by what executives called “extraordinary” data center leasing momentum, significantly outperforming its broader private equity and real estate holdings. “Despite all the negative things you’re reading about AI today, when we look across our business, this continues to be the area where we’re driving the highest returns,” Gray said during the call. But it’s hard to ignore the fact that the financing concerns and roadblocks threatening the broader AI infrastructure buildout are also hitting closer to home for Blackstone. Fears about rising financing costs have sent CoreWeave’s stock and bond prices plunging—the neocloud’s shares closed down another 10% Thursday after sliding last week—while Australian AI cloud provider Firmus abruptly pulled its initial public offering earlier this month. Blackstone has provided billions in loans to CoreWeave and has both invested in and lent money to Firmus. Blackstone has also been pressing ahead with brand-new AI ventures. In May, the firm announced an initial $5 billion equity commitment to a joint venture with Google to create a new cloud company that will use Google’s TPU chips, with plans to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by next year. The venture could need as much as $25 billion in total investment, including some borrowed money, and it has reportedly encountered delays at potential data center sites. Blackstone, for its part, says that broader anxiety about AI hasn’t undermined its ability to raise fresh cash for making its own investments. “We’re continuing to be able to raise capital. Obviously investors are asking the same question around AI, but what we continue to see is demand and usage of the AI going up faster than the compute,” Gray said. While Blackstone says it wants to continue going big in AI, it can only finance a tiny portion of the industry’s broader infrastructure buildout itself. The trillions of dollars of financing needed for chips and data centers in the coming years requires raising money from a far broader pool of investors. Blackstone itself has said it’s not clear where all the money will come from. Jas Khaira, the head of the team leading Blackstone’s push into AI investment, said late last month that the firm is still trying to determine which investors across the public debt and private credit markets will be able to provide the funding needed to sustain the buildout. “We have not mapped out who’s going to buy all the debt. We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don’t know where all of it will come from,” he said at The Information’s AI Agenda event in San Francisco. Data Center Headwinds Despite Blackstone’s overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers. —Nick Wingfield In Other News Meta Platforms’ stock fell 7% as investor enthusiasm over its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday gave way to concerns about the probability that it will need to issue new equity to pay for its AI spending. Andreessen Horowitz renamed its flagship blockchain fund a16z Frontier, dropping “crypto” from its name (The Information’s earlier scoop on the change is here ). Google partnered with energy company Voltus to pay homes and businesses to use less electricity during periods of peak demand. Data Center Headwinds

Despite Blackstone’s overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers.—Nick Wingfield
